topics.title: --add-dir
topics.description: `--add-dir` grants write access to an extra directory alongside the main workspace. You can repeat it for several paths. It is the usual fix when a task needs to edit a sibling package or a shared folder outside the project root.
resources: CLI flag combinations and safety tips

topics.title: --ask-for-approval
topics.description: `--ask-for-approval` (or `-a`) sets when Codex pauses for your approval before running a command. The values are `on-request`, where Codex works inside the sandbox and asks before going beyond it, and `never`, where it does not ask. It is the flag form of the `approval_policy` setting.
resources: CLI flag combinations and safety tips

topics.title: --cd
topics.description: `--cd` (or `-C`) sets the working directory Codex uses before it starts. It lets you launch Codex on a project without first changing folders in your shell. The directory becomes the workspace for file access and the sandbox.

topics.title: --help
topics.description: `--help` prints the commands and options available in your installed version. It is the most reliable reference, because the list of flags and slash commands changes between releases. Add it after a subcommand, such as `codex exec --help`, to see that command's own options.

topics.title: --image
topics.description: `--image` (or `-i`) attaches one or more images to the first prompt. Separate several paths with commas or repeat the flag. It is useful for error screenshots, design mockups and diagrams, as in `codex -i screenshot.png "Explain this error"`.

topics.title: --model
topics.description: `--model` (or `-m`) overrides the configured model for one run, for example `codex -m gpt-6.1-sol`. The same setting can be made permanent with `model` in `config.toml`. Inside a session, `/model` changes it without restarting.

topics.title: --profile
topics.description: `--profile` (or `-p`) loads a named profile on top of your base configuration. The profile is a `profile-name.config.toml` file in your Codex home directory. Profiles let you switch between setups, such as a strict one for production repos and a relaxed one for experiments.

topics.title: --sandbox
topics.description: `--sandbox` (or `-s`) selects the sandbox policy for commands that Codex runs. The options are `read-only`, `workspace-write` and `danger-full-access`. Most local work uses `workspace-write`, which allows edits inside the workspace but limits everything else.
resources: CLI flag combinations and safety tips

topics.title: --search
topics.description: `--search` turns on live web search for the run. By default, local Codex sessions use a cached search index, which lowers the risk of prompt injection from web pages. Live search fetches current pages, so treat the results as untrusted input.

topics.title: --worktree
topics.description: `--worktree` starts Codex in a new managed Git worktree. The changes stay isolated from your current checkout, so you can run a task without touching unfinished work. It works for new interactive sessions, `codex fork`, and `codex exec`.

topics.title: --yolo
topics.description: `--yolo` is the short form of `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`. It runs every command without approvals and without a sandbox, so Codex can change anything your user account can. Use it only inside an environment that is already isolated, such as a disposable container. For fewer prompts with more safety, use `--approve-for-me` instead.
resources: CLI flag combinations and safety tips

topics.description: Typing `@` opens a fuzzy file search in the composer. Choosing a result inserts that file path into your prompt, so Codex looks at exactly the file you mean. The `/mention` command does the same for files and folders.

Starting a prompt with `!` runs the rest as a local shell command instead of sending it to the model. The command runs under your current approval and sandbox settings. Use it for quick checks, such as `!git status`, without leaving Codex.

topics.title: AGENTS.md
topics.description: `AGENTS.md` is a markdown file with persistent instructions for Codex. A global file lives in your Codex home folder, and project files live from the repository root down to your working directory. An `AGENTS.override.md` in the same folder takes precedence over `AGENTS.md`. Codex stops reading once the combined size reaches 32 KiB by default, so keep the files short and split detail into nested folders.
resources: OpenAI Codex Tutorial #6 - Using the AGENTS.md file

topics.title: API usage
topics.description: You can sign in to Codex with an OpenAI API key instead of a ChatGPT account. API usage is billed at standard API rates and follows the models available to your key. Cloud features such as GitHub code review and Slack are not available with an API key. API keys are also the recommended way to authenticate Codex in CI.

topics.title: apply
topics.description: `codex apply` applies the latest diff from a Codex Cloud task to your local working tree. You pass the task ID, and the command is also available as `codex a`. Use it to bring cloud results into your local checkout after you have reviewed them.

topics.title: Approval Policies
topics.description: The approval policy controls when Codex stops to ask you. The supported values are `on-request`, where Codex works inside the sandbox and asks before going beyond it, and `never`, where it does not ask. A separate setting, `approvals_reviewer`, decides who answers: you, or an automatic reviewer agent with `auto_review`. That second option is what the "Approve for me" profile uses.
resources: Codex CLI approval_policy Configuration: on-request, never, Granular Policies, and Rules

topics.title: /approve
topics.description: `/approve` retries one recent action that automatic review denied. When Approve for me is on, a reviewer agent can reject a request. If you disagree, `/approve` lets you allow that single action without changing your settings.

topics.title: Archive & Delete
topics.description: Archiving hides a saved session from the picker without deleting it, and you can restore it with `codex unarchive`. Deleting removes the session permanently, including its descendants. Use `codex archive`, `codex delete`, or `/archive` and `/delete` inside a session.

topics.title: Astra
topics.description: GPT-6 Astra (`gpt-6-astra`) is the most capable model available in Codex. It is built for complex work across code, apps and research that needs sustained reasoning and judgment. It also has the smallest usage allowance, so keep it for the tasks that need it.

topics.title: Basic Workflows
topics.description: Most Codex work follows a few repeatable patterns: exploring a codebase, writing a good prompt, planning before editing, fixing bugs and reviewing the diff. Each pattern works the same in the CLI, the app and the IDE. Start with the one that matches your task, and use `/plan` and `/review` to add structure.

topics.title: Choosing Models
topics.description: Choose a model by the kind of task. Use Astra for the hardest reasoning, Sol for long-running work at a lower cost, Terra for visual and computer-use tasks, and Luna for narrow, high-volume jobs. Set it with `/model`, `--model` or `config.toml`. Subagents inherit the parent's model unless you set another one.

topics.title: CI/CD
topics.description: Codex can run inside your CI/CD pipeline to review pull requests, apply patches or generate reports. The usual building blocks are `codex exec` for the non-interactive run and the official GitHub Action. Authenticate with an API key stored as a secret, keep the sandbox as strict as the job allows, and treat pull request text as untrusted input.
resources: Codex Exec in CI: Practical Guide to Headless OpenAI Agents

topics.title: CLI
topics.description: The Codex CLI is a coding agent that runs locally in your terminal. You start it with `codex` inside a project, describe a task, and Codex inspects the code, edits files and runs your tools. It also supports sessions, code review, non-interactive runs with `codex exec`, skills, MCP servers and subagents. The CLI is open source under the Apache-2.0 license.

topics.title: Code Review
topics.description: Codex can review code at several points. `/review` and `codex review` check local changes, such as uncommitted work, a branch against its base or a single commit, and report findings without editing files. On GitHub, Codex can review pull requests automatically, and you can also request a review by commenting `@codex review`. The same cloud review works for GitLab merge requests.
resources: How to Use Codex CLI for Code Review
Code review is no longer the bottleneck

topics.title: Codex cloud
topics.description: Codex Cloud runs coding tasks on remote infrastructure instead of your machine. You create an environment with your repositories, setup scripts, internet access rules and secrets, then send a task to it. Each task gets its own workspace and keeps running while your computer sleeps. You review the changed files and test results, then commit or open a pull request, or apply the diff locally with `codex apply`.

topics.title: Codex Models
topics.description: Codex works with the GPT-6 model family, and each model suits a different kind of work. Astra is the most capable, Sol handles long-running work at a lower cost, Terra is fast with strong visual understanding and computer use, and Luna is the most efficient for high-volume tasks. You pick one with `/model`, the `--model` flag, or `model` in `config.toml`. Model names and retirements change often, so check the models page for the current list.

topics.title: codex
topics.description: `codex` starts the interactive terminal UI in the current directory. You can pass an optional starting prompt, for example `codex "explain this project"`, and attach images with `--image`. Run it from the root of the project you want to work on, because Codex uses the working directory as its workspace.

topics.title: /compact
topics.description: `/compact` summarizes the visible chat to free up context. Codex keeps the key points and drops the detail, so a long session can continue without hitting the context limit. Use it after long runs or when responses start to lose track of earlier work.

topics.title: config.toml
topics.description: `config.toml` is Codex's main settings file, found at `~/.codex/config.toml`. A trusted project can add its own `.codex/config.toml` for project-specific settings. It holds the model, sandbox mode, approval policy, MCP servers, hooks and many other options. The CLI, desktop app and IDE extension share it, and `--config` overrides a value for one run.
resources: Codex config.toml (2026): Add Any Custom Provider in 6 Lines

topics.title: /copy
topics.description: `/copy` copies the latest completed Codex output to your clipboard. Use it to take a finished answer or plan without selecting text manually. `Ctrl+O` does the same.

topics.title: Ctrl+C
topics.description: `Ctrl+C` interrupts what Codex is doing in the terminal UI. Use it to stop a turn that is going in the wrong direction. It is also commonly used to leave the session, as an alternative to `/exit`.

topics.title: Ctrl+G
topics.description: `Ctrl+G` opens the current prompt in your external editor, as set by the `$VISUAL` or `$EDITOR` environment variable. This is useful for writing long, multi-line prompts with your usual editing tools. When you save and close the editor, the text returns to the composer.

topics.title: Ctrl+L
topics.description: `Ctrl+L` clears and redraws the terminal screen without starting a new conversation. Your chat and context stay as they are, so it only cleans up the display. Use `/clear` instead when you want a fresh chat.

topics.title: Ctrl+O
topics.description: `Ctrl+O` copies the latest completed Codex output to your clipboard. It is the keyboard shortcut for `/copy`. Use it to grab a finished response or plan without selecting text by hand.

topics.title: Ctrl+R
topics.description: `Ctrl+R` opens a search through your prompt history. You type part of an earlier prompt and Codex shows matches you can reuse. It saves retyping long instructions you have used before.

topics.title: Custom Agents
topics.description: Custom agents are subagents you define yourself in a standalone TOML file. Put them in `~/.codex/agents/` for personal use or `.codex/agents/` for a project. Each file needs a `name`, a `description` and `developer_instructions`, and it can set a model and reasoning effort. A custom agent with the same name as a built-in one takes precedence. Custom agents inherit the parent's sandbox and approval settings and cannot override them.

topics.title: Customization
topics.description: Customization lets you extend Codex beyond its built-in behavior. Skills package repeatable workflows, MCP connects external tools and data, plugins bundle both for sharing, and `config.toml` holds your settings. Start with `AGENTS.md` and a few skills, and add integrations only when you need them.

topics.title: Desktop
topics.description: The ChatGPT desktop app is a graphical home for Codex on macOS, Windows and Linux. It lets you run several projects in parallel, keeps every chat visible and supports scheduled tasks, worktrees, browser use and computer use. You can start it from the terminal with `codex app`, or continue a CLI session in it with `/app`.

topics.title: /diff
topics.description: `/diff` shows the Git diff of the working tree, including files Git does not track yet. Use it to check what Codex changed before you commit or run tests. It works inside a Git repository.

topics.title: doctor
topics.description: `codex doctor` generates a diagnostic report about your setup. It checks the installation, configuration, authentication, runtime and Git health. Run it first when something is not working, and add `--json` if you want machine-readable output.

topics.title: Editor Extensions
topics.description: The Codex IDE extension works beside your code in the editor. It can use your open files, selected code and recent chats as context, and you review its edits in place. It supports VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf and VS Code Insiders, while Xcode and JetBrains IDEs have their own integrations. Plugins are not available in the extension.

topics.title: Esc + Esc
topics.description: Pressing `Esc` twice on an empty composer lets you edit your previous message. Pressing it again goes further back through earlier messages. When you send the edited message, the chat continues from that point as a fork, which is a quick way to correct a prompt that went wrong.

topics.title: exec
topics.description: `codex exec` runs Codex non-interactively, so you can use it in scripts and CI. Progress goes to stderr and the final message goes to stdout, which makes it easy to pipe. Useful flags include `--json` for JSONL events, `--output-schema` for structured results and `-o` to save the last message to a file. Runs are read-only by default unless you pick another sandbox.

topics.title: Explore Codebases
topics.description: Codex can read a repository and explain how it is organized before you change anything. Ask it for an overview, to trace where a feature is implemented, or to list the files involved in a bug. This is read-only work, so it is a safe way to start in an unfamiliar project. Use a read-only sandbox if you want to be sure nothing changes.

topics.title: Fast Mode
topics.description: Fast mode is a service tier that returns results sooner at a higher credit cost. You toggle it with `/fast` when the current model offers it. On eligible plans, Sol also has an Ultrafast tier. Use these modes when you are waiting on the answer, and leave them off for background or overnight work.
resources: Is Codex Fast Mode Worth It? 2.5x the Credits for 1.5x the Speed (I Tested It Live)

topics.title: /fast
topics.description: `/fast` toggles the Fast service tier for models that offer one. Fast mode returns results sooner but uses more credits, so it fits work you are waiting on. The setting persists until you switch it off.

topics.title: Fix Bugs & Refactoring
topics.description: For bug fixes, give Codex the error message, the steps to reproduce it and the expected behavior. It can find the cause, apply a fix and run the tests to confirm. For refactoring, state what must stay the same and what the target structure is, and ask it to keep the test suite passing. Review each change in the diff before accepting it.

topics.title: /fork
topics.description: `/fork` copies the current chat into a new one. The original transcript stays untouched, so you can try a different approach and still go back. Use it before a risky change or when you want to compare two solutions.

topics.title: Forking
topics.description: Forking copies a session into a new chat and keeps the original transcript unchanged. Use `codex fork` or `/fork` to try another approach without losing the first one. It is also useful for branching off a long session that has useful context.

topics.title: Git Checkpoints
topics.description: A Git checkpoint is a commit or stash you make before and after a Codex task. The docs recommend creating them so you can revert if the changes go wrong. Codex edits real files in your working tree, so a clean starting point makes review and rollback simple. Worktrees give a stronger form of isolation for bigger tasks.

topics.title: Git Worktrees
topics.description: A Git worktree is a second checkout of the same repository, so each task gets its own files and branch. Codex can create one for you: start with `codex --worktree`, use `/worktree` in a session, or run a scheduled task in a background worktree. This keeps parallel tasks from overwriting each other and keeps experiments away from your unfinished work.
resources: Codex App: Worktrees, Automations and Your First Commit
Codex App Worktrees: A Practical Workflow
Codex Multi-Agent Workflow with Git Worktrees

topics.title: GitHub Actions
topics.description: The `openai/codex-action@v1` action installs the Codex CLI and runs `codex exec` inside a GitHub workflow. You give it a prompt or a prompt file, a sandbox setting and your API key from a repository secret, and it returns the final message as an output. By default only users with write access can trigger it, and the docs advise sanitizing pull request text and running Codex as the last step of a job.
resources: How to Set Up AI Code Review in GitHub Actions
AI Fixed My Code While I Slept! (OpenAI Codex + Github Actions)

topics.title: /goal
topics.description: `/goal` sets, edits, pauses, resumes, shows or clears a task goal. The goal text works as both the first prompt and the completion criteria, so Codex keeps working until the outcome is reached. A good goal states the result, the constraints and how to verify it, such as a passing test suite. It keeps the same sandbox and approval settings, and pauses when it needs a decision.

topics.title: /hooks
topics.description: `/hooks` shows and manages lifecycle hooks. Hooks that you did not manage yourself must be reviewed and trusted here before they run, and a changed hook needs a new review. You can also disable hooks that are not enforced by an admin.

topics.title: Hooks
topics.description: Hooks run your own scripts at points in Codex's lifecycle. Events include `SessionStart`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PermissionRequest`, `PostToolUse`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop` and `Stop`. A hook receives JSON on stdin and can add context, allow or deny an action, or block a result. They are defined in `hooks.json` or in `config.toml`, and you must review and trust a hook with `/hooks` before it runs.
resources: Hooks vs. Skills in Codex Plugins
Hooks in Codex: What They Are and How to Use
Codex Hooks Reference: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Examples

topics.title: Images & Web Search
topics.description: Codex accepts images and can search the web. Add screenshots, designs or diagrams with `--image`, by pasting into the composer, or by dragging a file in. Web search uses a cached index by default in local sessions, and `--search` or `web_search = "live"` switches to live results. Treat all web results as untrusted input, because live pages can contain prompt injection.
resources: Codex images: attach screenshots, generate images and know the limits

topics.title: /import
topics.description: `/import` brings a Claude Code or Cursor setup into Codex. It can import supported configuration, projects and chats into Codex configuration and local files. Use it when you are moving from another coding agent and do not want to start from scratch.

topics.title: /init
topics.description: `/init` generates an `AGENTS.md` scaffold in the current directory. The file gives Codex persistent instructions for the project, such as build and test commands and coding conventions. Run it once in a new repository, then edit the result.

topics.title: Initialize a Project
topics.description: Initializing a project means creating its first `AGENTS.md`. Run `/init` in the project directory and Codex generates a scaffold you can edit. Review it, remove anything generic, and add the real build commands and rules of your repository.

topics.title: Integrations
topics.description: Codex connects to the tools where your team already works. On GitHub it can review pull requests automatically and respond to `@codex` mentions, and it can also start tasks from issues. It also works in GitLab (beta), Slack and Linear, where you can assign or mention Codex on an issue. Most of these integrations run in the cloud and need a ChatGPT plan rather than an API key.

topics.title: Introduction
topics.description: Codex is OpenAI's coding agent. It reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands and tests, and reports what it changed. You can use it from the terminal with the open-source Codex CLI, in the ChatGPT desktop app, in your editor, on the web and from your phone. All of these surfaces share the same agent and much of the same configuration.
resources: OpenAI Codex Crash Course – Build & Deploy Apps with Autonomous AI

topics.title: login
topics.description: `codex login` signs you in. It supports ChatGPT OAuth, device auth for remote or headless machines with `--device-auth`, an API key piped in with `--with-api-key`, and an access token with `--with-access-token`. `codex login status` shows the active auth mode and exits with code 0 when you are logged in.

topics.title: logout
topics.description: `codex logout` removes the stored credentials from your machine. Use it on shared computers or when you want to switch accounts. After logging out, the next `codex` run asks you to sign in again.

topics.title: Luna
topics.description: GPT-6 Luna (`gpt-6-luna`) is the most cost-efficient model, meant for focused, high-volume tasks such as summarization, extraction and narrow coding jobs. It has by far the largest usage allowance. The docs suggest it for fast, narrow subagent tasks.

topics.title: Manage Context
topics.description: The context window is the amount of information the model can consider at once. Long sessions fill it, and quality can drop as old details crowd out new ones. Compaction summarizes older context so work can continue, and `/compact` triggers it. `/status` shows token usage, `/recap` summarizes without compacting, and `/new` starts clean.
resources: Codex Context Window: Limits, Compaction, and AGENTS.md

topics.title: mcp
topics.description: `codex mcp` manages MCP servers from the command line. The subcommands `add`, `get`, `list`, `login`, `logout` and `remove` cover the whole lifecycle, including OAuth sign-in for remote servers. Servers are saved in `config.toml`, so the CLI, desktop app and IDE extension share them.

topics.title: /mcp
topics.description: `/mcp` lists the MCP tools configured for the session, and adding `verbose` shows server details. Use it to check which external tools Codex can call. Servers themselves are added with `codex mcp add`.

topics.title: MCP
topics.description: The Model Context Protocol connects Codex to external tools and data. Each server has a `[mcp_servers.<name>]` table in `config.toml`, and it is either a local STDIO process or a remote streamable HTTP server with OAuth or a bearer token. You add servers with `codex mcp add`. Per-server and per-tool approval settings control when Codex must ask before calling a tool.
resources: OpenAI Codex CLI with the Bright Data MCP Server

topics.title: /memories
topics.description: `/memories` configures how Codex uses and generates memory. You can turn memory injection or memory generation on or off without leaving the terminal UI. Memories are information Codex keeps across sessions, in addition to the instructions you write in `AGENTS.md`.

topics.title: /mention
topics.description: `/mention` attaches a file or folder to the chat. Codex then looks at exactly what you point to instead of searching for it. Typing `@` in the composer gives the same result with file search.

topics.title: Mobile
topics.description: The ChatGPT mobile app lets you start and follow Codex tasks from your phone. You can run a task in Codex Cloud or control a project on your own computer after pairing it with a QR code. From the app you can send new instructions, approve or deny commands, and review diffs and test results. The docs describe the iOS app, and availability depends on rollout and workspace settings.

topics.title: /model
topics.description: `/model` chooses the active model and, when the model supports it, the reasoning effort. Use it to move to a stronger model for a hard task or a cheaper one for simple work. The change applies to the current session.

topics.title: Models & Usage
topics.description: Models and usage decide how well Codex performs and how fast you use your allowance. Larger models and higher reasoning effort give better results on hard tasks but use more of your limits. Smaller models are faster and cheaper for simple work. Match the setting to the task, and watch your usage with `/usage` and `/status`.

topics.title: /new
topics.description: `/new` starts a new chat inside the same CLI session. The context is reset, but you stay in the same terminal and repository. `/clear` does a similar thing and also clears the terminal.

topics.title: Non-Interactive Mode
topics.description: Non-interactive mode runs Codex without the terminal UI through `codex exec`. You pass a prompt as an argument or through stdin, and Codex runs the task and prints the final message. It supports JSONL output, structured output with a JSON Schema, resuming earlier runs, and read-only defaults. In CI, set `CODEX_API_KEY` only for the command that needs it.
resources: Codex Exec: Run OpenAI Codex Safely from the Terminal
Codex Exec in CI: Practical Guide to Headless OpenAI Agents

topics.title: Parallel Sessions
topics.description: You can run several Codex chats at the same time, each with its own context. Parallel chats should not edit the same files, so give each one a separate worktree or a separate part of the code. Avoid giving two tasks write access to the same connected source. The desktop app and `codex agents` help you track many sessions in one place.
resources: How to Run Multiple Codex CLI Sessions at Once
Codex CLI multiple sessions: parallel work without branch chaos
OpenAI Codex Tutorial #11 - Running Tasks in Parallel

topics.title: Permissions & Approvals
topics.description: Permissions decide what Codex can do without asking you. Two settings work together: the sandbox limits what commands can read, write and reach, and the approval policy decides when Codex must pause for your confirmation. You choose a combination through permission profiles such as Ask for approval, Approve for me and Full access. Start with the most restrictive setting that lets you work.

topics.title: /permissions
topics.description: `/permissions` changes what Codex can do without asking, in the middle of a session. You can switch between profiles such as Ask for approval, Approve for me and Full access. Tighten it for risky work and relax it when you trust the task.

topics.title: Plan, Edit & Test
topics.description: For anything beyond a small change, ask Codex to plan first with `/plan`, then let it edit, then have it run the tests. Planning surfaces misunderstandings before they become code. Giving Codex a test command lets it check its own work and fix failures in the same turn.

topics.title: /plan
topics.description: `/plan` switches Codex to plan mode, optionally with a prompt. Codex proposes an approach before it changes anything, so you can correct the direction first. For long tasks, plan first and then turn the result into a goal with `/goal`.

topics.title: /plugins
topics.description: `/plugins` lists installed and discoverable plugins. From there you can inspect a plugin's tools, install one from a configured marketplace, or turn it on or off. Start a new session after installing before you use the plugin's skills or tools.

topics.title: Plugins
topics.description: A plugin is an installable bundle of capabilities. It can include skills, MCP server connections, hooks and browser extensions, and it is distributed through a marketplace shared by ChatGPT and Codex. In the CLI you open `/plugins` or use `codex plugin` to install from a configured marketplace. Start a new session after installing so the plugin's skills and tools load.
resources: Best Codex Plugins and Tools to Up Your Productivity in 2026
Codex Plugins Just Dropped: Skills, Apps, and MCP in One Place

topics.title: Project Conventions
topics.description: Project conventions are the rules Codex should follow when it works in your repository. Typical entries are how to run tests and linters, naming and formatting rules, folders that should not be edited, and what a good pull request looks like. Add a rule when you notice Codex repeating the same mistake. Put folder-specific rules in a nested `AGENTS.md` close to the code.

topics.title: Project Instructions
topics.description: Project instructions give Codex standing guidance so you do not repeat yourself in every prompt. They live in `AGENTS.md` files that Codex reads at the start of a run. Use them for how to build and test, the conventions to follow and the rules specific to a folder. Codex combines files from the project root down to your current directory, with nearer files taking precedence.

topics.title: Reasoning Efforts
topics.description: Reasoning effort controls how much reasoning budget the model uses before answering. Higher effort helps with planning and hard debugging, and lower effort reduces latency and cost. The levels run from low to extra high, and the options depend on the model. Change it with `/model` or `model_reasoning_effort` in `config.toml`.
resources: Codex Thinking Effort Guide: Levels, Models, Max vs Ultra

topics.title: /recap
topics.description: `/recap` generates a summary of the current conversation without compacting it. Your context stays intact, and you get a short catch-up on what has happened. It is handy when you return to a long session.

topics.title: /resume
topics.description: `/resume` opens your saved chats and resumes the one you pick. Use it to continue earlier work without leaving the terminal UI. The command-line equivalent is `codex resume`.

topics.title: resume
topics.description: `codex resume` continues a previous interactive session. Run it alone to pick from your saved sessions, add `--last` for the most recent one, or pass a session ID. Use `codex exec resume` for sessions started non-interactively.

topics.title: Resuming
topics.description: Resuming reopens a saved session with its context. Use `codex resume` to pick one, `codex resume --last` for the most recent, or `/resume` inside the terminal UI. This lets you continue work across days without explaining the task again.

topics.title: Review Diffs
topics.description: Reviewing the diff is how you stay in control of what Codex changed. Use `/diff` to see all edits, including new files, and `/review` to have a separate reviewer check them. You can also run `codex review` from the command line on uncommitted changes, a branch or a commit. Read the changes yourself before you commit.

topics.title: /review
topics.description: `/review` asks Codex to review your working tree. A dedicated reviewer reads the selected diff, such as uncommitted changes or a branch against its base, and reports prioritized findings without editing files. You can set `review_model` in `config.toml` to use a different model for reviews.

topics.title: review
topics.description: `codex review` runs a non-interactive code review. You can point it at uncommitted changes with `--uncommitted`, at a branch diff with `--base`, or at a single commit with `--commit`, and you can add custom review instructions. Codex reports prioritized findings and does not change your working tree.

topics.title: Sandbox Modes
topics.description: The sandbox is an enforced boundary around the commands Codex runs. `read-only` lets Codex inspect files but not change them, `workspace-write` allows edits inside the workspace and routine local commands, and `danger-full-access` removes the limits on files and network. `workspace-write` is the default low-friction mode for local work. You can allow extra writable folders with `--add-dir`.
resources: A Deep Dive into Codex Windows Sandbox

topics.title: Scaling Codex
topics.description: Scaling Codex means running more work at once without the tasks colliding. You can use Git worktrees to give each task its own checkout, run several sessions in parallel, and delegate focused work to subagents. Parallel work is safest when each task writes to different files. Cloud tasks add another way to run work without using your machine.

topics.title: Sessions
topics.description: A session is a saved Codex conversation, including its context and history. Codex stores your sessions so you can come back to them, branch them and clean them up. You can resume the latest one, fork an earlier one into a new chat, and archive or delete the ones you no longer need.

topics.title: Setting Up
topics.description: To set up the Codex CLI, install it, run `codex` in a project folder and sign in. On macOS and Linux the install script is `curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh`, and a PowerShell script exists for Windows. You can also install with `npm install -g @openai/codex` or `brew install --cask codex`. When Codex starts for the first time, choose "Sign in with ChatGPT" or use an API key.

topics.title: /skills
topics.description: `/skills` lets you browse and select a local skill. Choosing one adds it to your prompt so Codex follows its instructions. You can also type `$` followed by the skill name to call a skill directly.

topics.title: Skills
topics.description: A skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md` file that teaches Codex a repeatable workflow. The file needs a `name` and a `description`, and it can include scripts, references and assets. Codex loads only the name and description at first, and reads the full file when the skill is selected or the task matches. You call one explicitly with `$skill-name` or `/skills`. Skills are found in `.agents/skills` in your repository, in your home folder, and in an admin location.
resources: Codex Skills 101: Build Reusable AI Workflows with SKILLS.md
Best Codex Skills That Add the Most Value in 2026
How to Build Codex Skills Better than 99% of People

topics.title: Slash Commands (/)
topics.description: Typing `/` in the composer opens the list of built-in slash commands. They control the session from inside the terminal UI: choosing a model, changing permissions, planning, reviewing, managing context and more. Type part of a name to filter the list, then press Enter to run it.

topics.title: Sol
topics.description: GPT-6.1 Sol (`gpt-6.1-sol`) is built for repeated, long-running work across code, apps and documents. The docs describe its performance as close to Astra at a lower cost. It is the model the subagent docs suggest for demanding work, and it gets Ultrafast mode on eligible plans.

topics.title: /status
topics.description: `/status` shows the current session configuration and token usage. It confirms the active model, approval policy, writable roots and how much context remains. Use it when Codex behaves unexpectedly or before a long task.

topics.title: Subagents
topics.description: Subagents are specialized agents that Codex spawns to work in parallel and report back. They keep noisy output such as logs and exploration notes out of the main thread. Built-in agents are `default`, `worker` and `explorer`, and you can ask Codex directly to spawn them. They suit read-heavy work like exploration and triage, and they use more tokens than a single agent. Write-heavy parallel work can cause edit conflicts.
resources: OpenAI Codex Subagents: Complete Beginner Guide

topics.title: /subagents
topics.description: `/subagents` switches the active subagent thread. When Codex spawns subagents, each one works in its own thread, and this command lets you inspect or continue one from the main session. The `/agents` command opens a broader view for browsing chats and agents.

topics.title: Subscription Plans
topics.description: Codex is included with ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Edu and Enterprise plans. Higher plans give more usage and add cloud features such as automatic code review and Slack. Usage is measured in estimated messages per five-hour window for each model, and Pro currently has no five-hour limit. When you reach the included limits, Plus and Pro users can buy credits.

topics.title: TAB
topics.description: Pressing `Tab` while Codex is running queues a follow-up prompt, slash command or `!` command to run after the current turn. This lets you line up the next instruction without interrupting the work. Pressing `Enter` instead injects the instruction into the running turn.

topics.title: Terra
topics.description: GPT-6.1 Terra (`gpt-6.1-terra`) is a fast, efficient model for clear writing, visual understanding and computer use. It suits tasks where Codex works from screenshots or acts across your browser and apps. It requires Codex CLI version 0.159.0 or later.

topics.title: update
topics.description: `codex update` checks for a newer Codex CLI version and applies it when your install supports self-update. If you installed with npm or Homebrew, you can also update through that package manager. Keeping the CLI current matters because newer models can require a minimum version.

topics.title: Usage Limits
topics.description: Included usage is measured in estimated messages per five-hour window for each model, and the numbers differ between Astra, Sol, Terra and Luna. Pro currently has no five-hour limit, and cloud tasks can use more allowance than local messages. When you run out, Plus and Pro users can buy credits. Check `/usage` and the usage dashboard for current figures, since the limits are estimates.
resources: Understanding ChatGPT and Codex usage limits
Codex Usage Limits and Pricing in 2026
Never hit your codex usage limit again!

topics.title: Using Codex
topics.description: Using Codex means giving it a task, watching it work and reviewing the result. You describe the outcome, Codex explores the code, makes changes and runs checks, and you approve or redirect it along the way. The same loop applies in the terminal, the desktop app and your editor. Permissions and the sandbox decide how much Codex can do before it asks.

topics.title: Ways to use Codex
topics.description: Codex runs on several surfaces that share the same agent. The CLI works in your terminal, the ChatGPT desktop app manages many projects at once, and editor extensions bring it beside your code. The web and mobile apps let you start and follow tasks from anywhere, and Codex Cloud runs tasks on remote infrastructure. Pick the surface that fits where you work, and move between them when needed.

topics.title: Web
topics.description: Codex on the web runs in your browser at [chatgpt.com](http://chatgpt.com). You sign in with your ChatGPT account, choose where Codex should work and send a task. Web tasks run in the cloud, so they can keep going after you close the page. You can review the results there and continue from other devices.

topics.title: What is a Coding Agent?
topics.description: A coding agent is an AI system that can write, test and debug code on its own to complete a task. Unlike autocomplete, it can read many files, run shell commands, see the results and decide what to do next. You describe the outcome, and the agent plans and carries out the steps while you review the work.

topics.title: What is Agentic Loop?
topics.description: An agentic loop is the cycle an agent repeats until a task is done. The model reasons over the current context, calls a tool such as reading a file or running a command, observes the result and decides on the next step. In Codex this loop is bounded by the sandbox and approval settings, so the agent pauses when it needs permission to go further.
resources: What Is an Agentic Loop? The New Meta for AI Coding Agents

topics.title: Write Effective Prompts
topics.description: An effective prompt states the goal, gives the context, names the constraints and says how to check the result. For code, that means reproduction steps, the files that matter, boundaries such as what not to change, and a test or command that proves it works. Short prompts are fine when the task is clear. You can steer a running task with follow-up messages.

topics.title: Your First Task
topics.description: A good first task is small and easy to check, such as asking Codex to explain the project or fix a failing test. Open a project folder, run `codex`, and give a clear prompt with the goal and how to verify it. Review the changes with `/diff`, and run the tests yourself or ask Codex to run them. Create Git checkpoints before and after the task so you can revert if needed.
